name: Worse-than-average effect
statement: On skills that hardly anybody has, people place themselves below the average person, by the same comparison that puts them above average on skills nearly everybody has.
meaning: This is a claim about placement in a ranking rather than about how good people think they are in absolute terms. On hard tasks the two come apart. Moore and Healy report that people overestimate their actual performance on difficult tasks while believing they are worse than others, and that both errors reverse on easy tasks. Someone can think they juggle better than they do and still put themselves in the bottom quarter of jugglers. The effect is the better-than-average effect read at the other end of a difficulty scale, so an account of one has to explain the other. Kruger's own explanation is that the comparison is egocentric: people start from their own skill and adjust too little for everyone else's.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Kruger set the below-average effect against the Lake Wobegon literature, and his abstract concludes that the tendency to see oneself as above average may not be as ubiquitous as once thought. He puts the label in quotation marks in his own title.

evidence: Kruger's Study 1 gave eight abilities of varying difficulty to 37 Cornell students, 8 men and 29 women, and asked them to rank themselves against their peers. Mean percentile estimates were 58.8 for using a mouse, 65.4 for driving, 64.0 for riding a bicycle and 61.5 for saving money. On the four difficult abilities they were 46.5 for telling jokes, 27.8 for playing chess, 26.5 for juggling and 24.8 for computer programming. Every figure but telling jokes differed from the 50th percentile. Those numbers and that sample description are read off Korbmacher, Kwan and Feldman's reproduction of Kruger's table, because the original paper is paywalled and was not obtained. Studies 2 and 3 substituted a single easy or difficult test for the domain list, and Study 3 added cognitive load, which the abstract reports made both directions worse. Zell, Strickhouser, Sedikides and Alicke found the same split in their meta-analysis of better-than-average studies. Across seven matched samples that measured both kinds of ability, easy abilities gave dz = 1.10 and hard abilities gave a worse-than-average effect of dz = -0.52, t = 36.84, p < .001. Those meta-analytic figures are read from the authors' accepted manuscript in the University of Southampton repository.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication found the effect on three of the four difficult abilities Kruger used, and on the fourth it failed in the original too.
replication.detail: Korbmacher, Kwan and Feldman recruited 756 US MTurk workers in 2020 and kept 691 after preregistered exclusions, against Kruger's 37 students. The 240 who saw Kruger's original wording rated themselves above the 50th percentile on all four easy abilities and below it on playing chess at 41.0, juggling at 32.0 and programming at 40.7, each p < .001. Telling jokes came out at 52.4 and did not differ from the midpoint, which is the exception Kruger reported. Across the eight domains the correlation between rated difficulty and comparative standing was r = -0.85, the figure in the field below. Rewording the domains moved the result as predicted: mean comparative ability was 58.86 under easy rewordings, 53.29 under the original wording and 46.97 under difficult ones. The egocentric pattern held as well. For driving, own absolute ability predicted comparative standing at a standardised beta of 0.85 where peers' ability predicted it at -0.11.

study.cite: Korbmacher, M., Kwan, C. (I.), & Feldman, G. (2022). Both better and worse than others depending on difficulty: Replication and extensions of Kruger's (1999) above and below average effects. Judgment and Decision Making, 17(2), 449-486.

limits: Difficulty is not the only thing that varies across these domains. In the replication the easy abilities were rated more desirable than the difficult ones by 1.16 scale points, and comparative standing tracked desirability at r = 0.72, 95% CI [0.03, 0.95]. The mechanism is disputed. Moore and Small argue that no bias is needed, because people hold better information about their own performance than about anyone else's, so their estimates of others regress further towards a prior. That alone puts people above average on easy tasks and below average on hard ones. Their third experiment takes the self out of the design. Participants judged two other people, and those shown one person's completed quiz predicted that person would beat the other by 0.66 points on an easy quiz and lose by 0.25 on a difficult one, while those shown the other person's quiz predicted the reverse, F(1, 109) = 13.24, p < .001. Chambers and Windschitl had concluded that differential regression plays no major role, a line Moore and Small quote from page 828 and answer by pointing to differences in how the two sets of studies measured performance. The meta-analytic estimate rests on seven matched samples. Zell and colleagues also report that their most stringent selection model drops the better-than-average effect for abilities from dz = 0.51 to 0.09, so the ability literature this effect lives in may be the part most exposed to publication bias. Moore's 2007 review of worse-than-average findings, in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, is paywalled and was not obtained for this entry.
misreadings: Believing oneself worse than average is not the same as believing one did badly. Moore and Healy report that on difficult tasks people overestimate their actual scores at the same time as they place themselves below others, so the two errors point in opposite directions in the same person. The effect is not evidence of low self-esteem or of modesty either, because the same participants show the opposite bias on the easy items of the same questionnaire. It is a different measurement from the hard-easy effect in calibration, which compares stated confidence against accuracy rather than the self against other people, and which has its own entry here. Kruger's finding does not overturn illusory superiority. Zell and colleagues put the pooled better-than-average effect at dz = 0.78 across 291 samples, and the reversal shows up in the ability domains where hardly anyone is skilled.
